Remember that a *unit* fraction is a fraction containing ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14129811/assets/ccee5f5be0445cce59832a3def74f395a7d05cc12dc630fb36baf8f3d2d448bd.svg) in the numerator. So, for example, the fractions 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14129811/assets/2e38b15a8f3be74e15b87e81264b66571e593de7250dc902aeaa0e7bc1c506bf.svg)
are both unit fractions, whereas 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14129811/assets/d157ce836a54214740d295f545d4c94d8c57d54d92ac7f075ed9b92556c932b1.svg)
are *not* unit fractions.

In this lesson, we will use models to divide unit fractions by whole numbers. 

Let's use a fraction model to find the value of 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14129811/assets/d8815c6716e962ce4aebee24d004d4c591a1bc35c5fdebcd87d26ace61ead7fb.svg)
We start with a square model of ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14129811/assets/9fcebe90d169f37bbdbf55f9e4ac86ceaf6ea6d573d101f382a12008bb0c5c2a.svg) split *vertically*.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14129811/assets/ccfe0f457342c456200c98cfc46e63bdc1153698282085164eeafae5c2092c45.png)

To divide ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14129811/assets/9ae11798da63cafee6ce5ccf824a7b96f9f7407a4ee445d1431d907c36f5dd1b.svg) by ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14129811/assets/dbfe30ca4e672459c180bd90f25f84f025162b8ce73260773fb1fbdf39b0a052.svg) we split the above whole into ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14129811/assets/6f33d8df0d08ae9bddce540bedf62f46e93e748e4a5b6fd85b1dc626953e44a6.svg) equal parts *horizontally*. Then, we remove any shaded parts that are not in the bottom row.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14129811/assets/7940073ba05d3136ee1d465530a60bc3624b7aa06fd7484d30797758a28976d7.png)

From the picture on the right, we obtain that the shaded part represents ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14129811/assets/42accbcb8cbfd14800ac4a27bc87d5ba529ff4173a91499f32705cd41b0c88b0.svg) of the whole.
